The '''quadratic integrate and fire''' ('''QIF''') '''model''' is a [[biological neuron model]] that describes [[action potentials]] in neurons. In contrast to physiologically accurate but computationally expensive neuron models like the [[Hodgkin–Huxley model]], the QIF model seeks only to produce action potential-like patterns by ignoring the dynamics of transmembrane currents and [[ion channels]]. Thus, the QIF model is computationally efficient and has found ubiquitous use in computational neuroscience.<ref>{{Citation |last=Fourcaud-Trocmé |first=Nicolas |title=Integrate and Fire Models, Deterministic |date=2013 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-7320-6_148-1 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Computational Neuroscience |pages=1–9 |editor-last=Jaeger |editor-first=Dieter |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-7320-6_148-1 |isbn=978-1-4614-7320-6 |access-date=2023-03-01 |editor2-last=Jung |editor2-first=Ranu|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The QIF model is related to the [[Theta model#Quadratic integrate-and-fire|Ermentrout–Kopell canonical "theta" model]] via a change of variables.

An idealized model of neural spiking is given by the [[autonomous differential equation]],

: <math>\frac{dx}{dt} = x^2 + I</math>

where <math>x</math> represents the membrane voltage and <math>I\geq 0</math> represents an input current. A solution to this differential equation is the function,<ref>{{cite book |last=Ermentrout |first1=Bard |last2=Terman |first2=David |title=Mathematical Foundations of Neuroscience |edition=1 |publisher=Springer |date=July 1, 2010 |isbn=978-0-387-87708-2 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-87708-2 }}</ref>

: <math>x(t) = \sqrt{I} \tan(\sqrt{I} t + c_0),</math>

where <math>c_0</math> is an arbitrary shift dependent on the initial condition <math>x(0)</math> (specifically by the formula <math>c_0 = \arctan(x(0)/\sqrt{I})</math>). This solution "blows up" in finite time, namely at <math>t=n\pi/(2\sqrt{I})-c_0</math> for all <math>n \in\mathbb{N}</math>, which resembles the rhythmic action potentials generated by neurons stimulated by some input current. Thus a "spike" is said to have occurred when the solution reaches positive infinity. Just after this point in time, the solution resets to negative infinity by definition.

When implementing this model in a numerical simulation, a threshold crossing value (<math>V_t</math>) and a reset value (<math>V_r</math>) is assigned, so that when the solution rises above the threshold, <math>x(t) \geq V_t</math>, the solution is immediately reset to <math>V_r</math>.

The above equation is directly related to an alternative form of the QIF model,

: <math>\frac{dv}{dt} = -\frac{v(1-v)}{\tau_m} + I </math>,

where <math>\tau_m</math> is the membrane time constant.
